preamble: Dilan is sitting on the chair outside the head teacher's office one Thursday afternoon. He tells us himself how he came to be there.
body:
I am not in trouble. I want that said before anybody starts, because people keep walking past this chair and doing the face at me.

The blue chair outside Mrs Farrell's office is a waiting chair. Farhan sat on it in March because he handed in a wallet with forty pounds in it, and they gave him a pencil with the school crest on and put his photograph up by the hatch. So.

What happens is, on Thursday I go past the Reception window at break and one of the butterflies has already come out. It is hanging under the card with its wings going, pumping them, which is the sign. You can look it up. If you leave them in the net after that they get sad and start bashing themselves against the sides, and I am not going to stand there and let that happen to a Reception butterfly while everybody else is playing football.

Miss Deller did say nobody was to open the net except her. She said it on Monday, though, and on Monday they were all still asleep in their chrysalises, so by Thursday the instruction is basically out of date. I check with Marnie first. Marnie says don't, Dilan. Marnie says don't about everything, including the water fountain last term, which dried out in the end and was fine.

The net will not carry flat, so I put four of them in my lunchbox for the journey, with the lid resting on top and not clicked down, obviously, because I am not stupid. Two ride on my sleeve the whole way and do not even try to get off. I would say they chose me. Nobody tells me the governors are in the hall.

It goes well, though. Mrs Kaur laughs. One of the governors holds his hand out flat and a butterfly sits on it for about a minute while he stays completely still, and he says something to the other one about a Painted Lady, so he knows what they are, which proves they were ready. Miss Deller thanks me. She thanks me three separate times, quite loudly, and then she sits down on the PE bench and has a long drink of water.

Reception are fine. Some of them are screaming, but that is just what Reception is like at half past two.

There are eleven and we have got seven back, which is more than half, so as a percentage it is a pass. Two are up on the beam over the stage where the ropes hang, and Mr Okafor says nobody is going up there for a butterfly, not today. One is on the fire extinguisher by the double doors and will not be moved. One went through the serving hatch into the kitchen, which is not ideal. I would rather not say what I think about the last one, because Mrs Farrell's office has a window in it that was open all afternoon.

My lunchbox is in there on her desk. She is keeping it safe for me.

Mum is in there as well. She came at half past two, which is early for her, and she did not say anything on the way past, she just did a small nod, which is our thing. I can hear her voice through the door doing the short answers. I can hear Mrs Farrell say the word "again", but that will be about the fountain, and the fountain was ages ago and everybody has moved on from it.

Anyway. When they come out I am going to explain about the wings, because I do not think Miss Deller had actually looked at them properly since Monday, and once you have seen one doing it you cannot really leave it in a net.

The handle is going down. There is a butterfly sitting on top of the doorframe, right above where Mrs Farrell's head is about to be, and I am the only person in this corridor who can see it, and I am not going to be the one who tells her.

I stand up, because you stand up when somebody is about to thank you.
